Which Group to Sample Next Under a Budget Constraint

Source: R/seq_budget.R
seq_budget_next.Rd

Given a check from seq_budget, returns the group that should receive the next observation, or NA when sampling has ended. Only a group whose next observation the remaining budget can pay for is ever returned, so a study that adds one observation at a time to the group named here cannot spend more than its budget.

Usage

seq_budget_next(check, order = c("shortfall", "rounds"))

Arguments

check

An object returned by seq_budget.

order

How the next group is chosen among those that still need an observation and can be paid for: "shortfall" (default) or "rounds"; an unambiguous abbreviation is accepted. See Details.

Value

A length one integer: the position in groups (as passed to seq_budget) of the group that should receive the next observation. It is NA when sampling has ended, which is exactly when the check's rule_met or budget_exhausted attribute is TRUE: either every group has met its criterion, or the remaining budget cannot pay for an observation from any group that has not. (That is also when is_satisfied is TRUE, unless the variance of a group is unusable.)

Details

A group is a candidate when it has not met its criterion (it still needs observations) and one more observation from it costs no more than what is left of the budget. If there is no candidate the function returns NA, and the check's rule_met and budget_exhausted attributes say why. A group that needs observations but cannot be paid for is passed over in favor of one that can, so the budget is used as fully as the unit costs allow.

Among the candidates:

order = "shortfall"

(the default, and the package's choice) the next observation goes to the group furthest below its estimated optimal size, that is, the one with the smallest ratio of its current size to its target in Equation 18 of Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal (2025). This keeps the allocation as close as possible to the estimated optimal one at every step.

order = "rounds"

the next observation goes to the candidate with the fewest observations. With equal pilot sizes this visits the open groups one at a time, in rounds, in decreasing order of their standard deviations, which is the order the article describes (Stage 2, pp. 429 to 430; one observation per group per stage). Combine it with the closed argument of seq_budget for the first passage rule.

Ties go to the group with the larger sample standard deviation and then to the one listed first.

A group whose variance is unusable, because every observation in it is equal, has no target to be measured against (the check marks it in not_estimable_per_group). Under either order it takes its turn by rounds: it is named when no group whose variance can be used has fewer observations than it has, and otherwise only when it is the one group that can still be sampled. It is never sampled ahead of the others, so a group that stays constant cannot draw the whole budget to itself; it does keep pace with the least sampled of the other groups, as the help for seq_budget explains. This rule is the package's choice: the article does not treat the case.

How the first passage option differs from the article. With closed and order = "rounds" the package follows the article's rule that a population is not sampled again once it has met its criterion, but three details differ. (1) The article orders the populations by their first stage standard deviations; a check does not know those, so the current ones are used. (2) The article's flowchart (Figure 1) ends the procedure at the first observation that cannot be paid for, and its text does not say whether a cheaper open group may still be sampled when a more expensive one can no longer be afforded; the package continues with the cheaper group, which uses the budget more fully and still cannot exceed it. (3) The article judges a population against its criterion only after an observation has been drawn from that population (Equations 16 and 17); a check judges every open group each time, so a group can be closed after an observation drawn from another group, sooner than the article would close it. The differences are small: in simulations of the normal row of the article's Table 1, the option ended with every group closed in 31 percent of studies where the article's own sequence, programmed separately, did in 29 percent; the mean final sample sizes differed by 0.3 or less and the mean cost by about 1 in a budget of 5,000. Even so, the option is the package's reading of the article's procedure, not a step for step copy of it.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., Bandyopadhyay, T., Kelley, K., & Padalunkal, J. J. (2025). A sequential approach for noninferiority or equivalence of a linear contrast under cost constraints. Psychological Methods, 30(2), 425–439. doi:10.1037/met0000570

seq_budget

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Scores after a new training format (group 1) and two existing formats;
# an observation costs 38, 15, and 10.
set.seed(113)
scores <- list(
  rnorm(10, mean = 52, sd = 9),
  rnorm(10, mean = 50, sd = 6),
  rnorm(10, mean = 50, sd = 6)
)
out <- seq_budget(scores, contrast_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),
                  cost_per_group = c(38, 15, 10), budget = 1500)
seq_budget_next(out)
#> [1] 1

# Near the end of a smaller study, 24 is left of a budget of 680. Group 1
# is still below its criterion but costs 38 per observation, so the next
# observation goes to group 3, which also needs one and costs 10.
set.seed(113)
scores <- list(
  rnorm(12, mean = 52, sd = 9),
  rnorm(8, mean = 50, sd = 6),
  rnorm(8, mean = 50, sd = 6)
)
out <- seq_budget(scores, contrast_weights = c(1, -0.5, -0.5),
                  cost_per_group = c(38, 15, 10), budget = 680)
attr(out, "remaining_budget")
#> [1] 24
attr(out, "met_per_group")
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE
seq_budget_next(out)
#> [1] 3
